html:
The Mahad Satyagraha was a protest on 20 March 1927 in the town of Mahad in western India, where B. R. Ambedkar led thousands of Dalits, then called untouchables, to drink water from a public tank closed to them.

The Bombay legislature had already declared in 1923 that public water sources were open to all, and Mahad's town council had agreed. But caste Hindus kept Dalits away from the Chavdar tank. Ambedkar walked to the tank and drank, and the crowd followed. Caste Hindu mobs then attacked them. Afterwards priests "purified" the tank with cow products.

Ambedkar came back in December 1927 for a second conference. There his followers publicly burned the Manusmriti, an ancient law book that set out caste duties and the low status of untouchables and women. Dalit groups still mark the day.

A court case over the tank ran for years before the courts sided with the Dalits. The protest came soon after the Vaikom Satyagraha over road access in Kerala. Two decades later Ambedkar chaired the drafting of the Constitution of India, which abolished untouchability.
sum: The Mahad Satyagraha was a protest on 20 March 1927 in the town of Mahad in western India, where B. R. Ambedkar led thousands of Dalits, then called untouchables, to drink water from a public tank closed to them.
